o1.biggest_strength: Every angle and hook decision is tied back to the owner's own cost-per-purchase numbers, and the hook test gives a real money rule (about $520 per hook at $26 CPA, keep under $32), which a small team can run tomorrow.
o1.biggest_mistake: The blanket 'must say all three approved claims word for word' instruction risks creators cramming all three into 40 seconds, and the closing 'To confirm: creator fees and shoot dates' is a small piece of homework for an owner who said they are unavailable.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Make the claims instruction explicit per script (which claims belong in which ad) so creators don't cram, and close it as a finished brief with no open items.

o2.biggest_strength: The cleanest, most natural-reading scripts of the two, with the 'A new kind of soda' tagline closing every ad and consistent rules that keep taste first and the label late.
o2.biggest_mistake: The hook test plan is too vague to act on: 'run all nine at the same budget, after about a week compare' gives no purchases-per-hook or cost thresholds, so the team cannot judge a winner reliably.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add a money-based testing rule (purchases per hook, cost per purchase against $26/$32) and usage-rights/delivery terms so the creator briefs are complete.

reason: Both give three strong, on-data scripts with correct numbers and disclosure, but Output 1 is the one I can hand to a producer and media buyer tomorrow: it includes the day-to-day hook rules with money math, delivery specs and usage terms, while Output 2's test plan is too loose to call a winner.
